passages.title: Paul defends the source of a message whose reception is now disputed
passages.summary: Paul writes to the assemblies of Galatia as an apostle sent by Jesus Christ. He gives no thanks. He is amazed that they are turning so quickly to a different good news. He says anyone who brings another message is cursed. His message did not come from a human source. He once persecuted the assembly and advanced in Judaism. God called him, and he went to Arabia, not to Jerusalem. After three years he visited Peter for fifteen days and saw James.
passages.uncertainty: Lines join the places Galatians names, in order. They do not trace real roads or sea lanes.

lds.text: The selected lesson studies the problem of turning toward another message. Why does Paul distinguish revelation from instruction by the earlier apostles?

contextNote.title: Paul defends the source of a message whose reception is now disputed
contextNote.text: Verse 11 says Paul’s good news is not of human origin. Verse 12 denies two human routes: he neither received it nor was taught it. It came through revelation of Jesus Christ. The rest of the chapter gives evidence from his movements. He did not consult anyone or go to Jerusalem (verses 16–17). His first visit came three years later and lasted fifteen days (verse 18). Verse 20 swears before God that this is no lie.

passages.title: Shared recognition fails when fear divides the meal
passages.summary: After fourteen years Paul goes to Jerusalem with Barnabas and Titus. Titus, a Greek, is not forced to be circumcised. James, Peter, and John give Paul and Barnabas the right hand of fellowship. They ask only that he remember the poor. In Antioch Peter eats with Gentiles, then draws back when men come from James. Barnabas is carried along too. Paul rebukes Peter before everyone. He says a person is justified by faith in Christ, not by law.
passages.uncertainty: Lines join the places Galatians names, in order. They do not trace real roads or sea lanes.

lds.text: How does Peter’s meal withdrawal conflict with the earlier shared recognition?

contextNote.title: Shared recognition fails when fear divides the meal
contextNote.text: Verse 12 gives the facts: Peter ate with Gentiles and then withdrew in fear. Verse 13 says the other Jewish believers and Barnabas followed him. Verse 14 names the fault: not walking by the truth of the good news. Paul answers “before them all.” His question points to the gap. Peter himself had lived like a Gentile. Now his withdrawal pressed Gentiles to live like Jews.

passages.title: Promise and shared inheritance answer the demand for another membership sign
passages.summary: Paul calls the Galatians foolish and asks how they received the Spirit. It was by hearing with faith, not by works of the law. Abraham believed God, and those of faith are his children. The law curses all who fail to keep it, and Christ redeemed us. The promise to Abraham came 430 years before the law. The law cannot cancel it. The law was a tutor to bring us to Christ. In Christ there is neither Jew nor Greek, slave nor free, male nor female.
passages.uncertainty: Markers show the cities Paul names in his memories. Mount Sinai and the Jerusalem above have no point.

lds.text: The selected lesson connects receiving the Spirit with the gospel’s freedom. Why can the later law not cancel Abraham’s earlier promise?

contextNote.title: Promise and shared inheritance answer the demand for another membership sign
contextNote.text: The dispute is who counts as Abraham’s offspring and heir. Verse 16 says the promised offspring is Christ. Verse 17 says the later law cannot cancel that promise. Verses 26–28 say all who are baptized into Christ are one in him. Verse 29 draws the conclusion in two steps. If they belong to Christ, they are Abraham’s offspring. If offspring, they are heirs by promise.

passages.title: Paul turns a family account into an argument about the disputed promise
passages.summary: Paul says an heir who is a child is no different from a servant. God sent his Son, born of a woman, to redeem those under the law. Now they are sons and call God Abba, Father. He asks why they turn back to weak principles and observe days and seasons. He recalls how they welcomed him when he was ill. He is in labor again until Christ is formed in them. Then he tells of Abraham’s two sons, by Hagar and by the free woman. He says believers are children of the free woman.
passages.uncertainty: Markers show the cities Paul names in his memories. Mount Sinai and the Jerusalem above have no point.

lds.text: The selected lesson studies Paul’s appeal against returning to bondage. Why must the two mothers’ roles here remain part of Paul’s stated comparison?

contextNote.title: Paul turns a family account into an argument about the disputed promise
contextNote.text: Verse 21 addresses those who want to be under the law. Paul answers them from the law’s own account of Abraham (verse 22). Verse 24 says plainly that he reads it as an allegory. The two women stand for two covenants, and Hagar stands for Sinai. Verse 26 sets the free Jerusalem above against her. This is Paul’s comparison for this dispute, not a verdict on a people. Verse 31 gives its point: believers are children of the free woman.

passages.title: Freedom becomes service through love rather than permission to consume others
passages.summary: Paul tells the Galatians to stand firm in freedom. If they accept circumcision, they must keep the whole law. What counts is faith working through love. He says a little yeast leavens the whole lump. They were called to freedom, to serve one another through love. The whole law is fulfilled in loving a neighbor as oneself. He lists the works of the flesh and then the fruit of the Spirit. The fruit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith, gentleness, and self-control.
passages.uncertainty: Markers show the cities Paul names in his memories. Mount Sinai and the Jerusalem above have no point.

lds.text: The selected lesson teaches freedom through love and conduct shaped by the Spirit. How does freedom become service rather than permission to harm others?

contextNote.title: Freedom becomes service through love rather than permission to consume others
contextNote.text: Verse 1 said Christ set them free and warned against a yoke of bondage. Verse 13 guards that freedom from the other side. Freedom must not become an opening for the flesh. The verse then tells free people to be servants to one another. Love is the means. Verse 14 gives the reason: the whole law is fulfilled in loving a neighbor. Verse 15 shows the alternative: biting and devouring until they consume each other.

passages.title: Shared burdens stand beside personal examination and patient work
passages.summary: Paul tells the spiritual to restore gently anyone caught in a fault. They should bear one another’s burdens. Each should test his own work and carry his own load. A person reaps what he sows, to the flesh or to the Spirit. They should not grow tired of doing good, especially to the household of faith. Paul writes the ending in large letters with his own hand. He says those pressing circumcision want to avoid persecution. He will boast only in the cross, and a new creation is what counts.
passages.uncertainty: Markers show the cities Paul names in his memories. Mount Sinai and the Jerusalem above have no point.

lds.text: The selected lesson teaches patient work and the later consequences of choices. How do shared burdens and personal examination support each other?

contextNote.title: Shared burdens stand beside personal examination and patient work
contextNote.text: Verse 1 gives a case: someone is caught in a fault. Those who restore him must be gentle and watch themselves. Verse 2 widens the case to a rule: bear one another’s burdens. It calls this fulfilling “the law of Christ.” The letter has argued against the law as a requirement for Gentiles. Here Paul names a law they do keep, and 5:14 called it love. Verse 5 adds that each still carries his own load.

places.uncertainty: The marker shows the city’s general location.

ancientRoads.title: Appian Way
ancientRoads.summary: The Appian Way joined Rome with Capua and the port of Brundisium. Rome began it in 312 BCE.
ancientRoads.detail: Acts 28:15 says believers met Paul at the Market of Appius and Three Taverns. Both were stops on this road south of Rome.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: The road’s course is well known. The line joins its main towns and smooths the bends.

ancientRoads.title: Via Egnatia
ancientRoads.summary: Rome built this road across Macedonia in the second century BCE. It ran from the Adriatic coast to Thessalonica and on to Byzantium.
ancientRoads.detail: Acts 16:11–17:1 takes Paul through Neapolis, Philippi, Amphipolis, Apollonia, and Thessalonica. The encyclopedia article places that trip on this road.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: Milestones mark the road as far as the edge of Thrace. The line joins known towns and smooths the bends.

ancientRoads.title: Via Sebaste
ancientRoads.summary: Rome finished this army road in 6 BCE. It climbed from Perga on the coast to Antioch of Pisidia. A branch reached Iconium and Lystra.
ancientRoads.detail: Acts 13:14 takes Paul from Perga to Antioch of Pisidia. He may have used this road, but Acts does not say.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: Milestones fix parts of the road. The line between the towns is simplified.

ancientRoads.title: Cilician Gates pass
ancientRoads.summary: This pass crosses the Taurus Mountains north of Tarsus. It joins the plain of Cilicia with the high plateau.
ancientRoads.detail: Armies and traders used the pass for a very long time. Acts 15:41 sends Paul through Cilicia but does not name the pass.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: The pass is certain. The line beyond it is a broad guide.

ancientRoads.title: International coastal highway
ancientRoads.summary: This major route linked Egypt with the coast and northern Levant. Traders, messengers, and imperial armies used its plains and passes.
ancientRoads.detail: The southern section followed the coast through Gaza and Philistia. Farther north, important branches crossed Carmel and the Jezreel Valley. “Via Maris” is a familiar later name. This guide calls it the international coastal highway. The line follows Iron Age evidence, not a first-century road study.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: The sources rebuild this route from Iron Age evidence, about 1200–587 BCE. This guide has not reviewed a first-century road study for it.

ancientRoads.title: Jezreel Valley–Damascus route
ancientRoads.summary: This branch connected Megiddo and the Jezreel Valley with Beth Shean. It continued toward the upper Jordan region and Damascus.
ancientRoads.detail: The valley and its crossings supported trade and army travel. The route joined the coast, Galilee, Transjordan, and inland Syria. The line follows Iron Age evidence, not a first-century road study.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: The sources rebuild this route from Iron Age evidence, about 1200–587 BCE. This guide has not reviewed a first-century road study for it.

ancientRoads.title: Beth-horon ascent
ancientRoads.summary: This important western route connected the coastal plain with Jerusalem. It passed through the Aijalon Valley and climbed Beth-horon.
ancientRoads.detail: The ascent used a favorable pass through difficult hill country. It served traffic between the coast, the Benjamin plateau, and Jerusalem. The line follows Iron Age evidence, not a first-century road study.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: The sources rebuild this route from Iron Age evidence, about 1200–587 BCE. This guide has not reviewed a first-century road study for it.

regions.name: Judea · Roman province
regions.summary: Rome removed Herod’s son Archelaus in 6 CE and made Judea a province. Its governor lived at Caesarea on the coast.
regions.detail: Governors Felix and Festus hold Paul at Caesarea (Acts 23–26). Acts 12 names an earlier ruler King Herod; historians call him Agrippa I.
regions.uncertainty: The shape joins Judea, Samaria, and Idumea. The province grew after 44 CE.

regions.name: Syria · Roman province
regions.summary: Rome made Syria a province in 64 BCE. It bordered the lands of Herod’s family on the north.
regions.detail: Believers are first called Christians at Antioch in Syria (Acts 11:26). Antioch sends out Barnabas and Saul in Acts 13.
regions.uncertainty: The shape is a simple guide to the province.

regions.name: Cilicia · approximate
regions.summary: Cilicia lay on the south coast of Asia Minor. Rome took it in 64 BCE.
regions.detail: Paul comes from Tarsus in Cilicia (Acts 21:39). He passes through Syria and Cilicia in Acts 15:41.
regions.uncertainty: The shape shows the eastern plain around Tarsus only.

regions.name: Cyprus · Roman province
regions.summary: Cyprus was a Roman province under a proconsul. Paphos was its capital.
regions.detail: Barnabas comes from Cyprus (Acts 4:36). He and Saul cross the island from Salamis to Paphos in Acts 13.
regions.uncertainty: The shape follows the modern coast of the island.

regions.name: Galatia · Roman province
regions.summary: Augustus made Galatia a province in 25 BCE. Ancyra was its capital.
regions.detail: Paul writes to the assemblies of Galatia. Acts 13–14 places him at Antioch of Pisidia, Iconium, Lystra, and Derbe.
regions.uncertainty: The shape is a simple guide. Pamphylia on the south coast belonged to Galatia for a time.

regions.name: Asia · Roman province
regions.summary: Asia was a rich Roman province in western Asia Minor. A proconsul governed it.
regions.detail: Paul teaches in Ephesus for two years (Acts 19:10). Revelation 1–3 writes to seven assemblies in Asia.
regions.uncertainty: The shape is a simple guide to the province.

regions.name: Bithynia and Pontus · Roman province
regions.summary: Rome joined Bithynia and Pontus into one province on the Black Sea coast.
regions.detail: The Spirit keeps Paul from entering Bithynia (Acts 16:7). First Peter greets believers in Pontus and Bithynia.
regions.uncertainty: The shape is a simple guide to the coast lands.

regions.name: Cappadocia · Roman province
regions.summary: Cappadocia became a Roman province in 17 CE. Its capital was a city named Caesarea.
regions.detail: People from Cappadocia hear Peter at Pentecost (Acts 2:9). First Peter 1:1 greets believers there.
regions.uncertainty: The shape is a simple guide. This Caesarea is not the port in Judea.

regions.name: Macedonia · Roman province
regions.summary: Rome made Macedonia a province in 146 BCE. The Via Egnatia crossed it from west to east.
regions.detail: A vision calls Paul to Macedonia (Acts 16:9). He teaches in Philippi, Thessalonica, and Beroea.
regions.uncertainty: The shape is a simple guide. It includes Thessaly and Epirus, which the province held.

regions.name: Achaia · Roman province
regions.summary: Achaia covered southern Greece. Augustus made it a province apart from Macedonia.
regions.detail: Paul speaks in Athens and stays in Corinth (Acts 17–18). Gallio, proconsul of Achaia, hears a charge against him.
regions.uncertainty: The shape is a simple guide. The province’s islands are not marked.

regions.name: Crete · part of a Roman province
regions.summary: Rome governed Crete together with Cyrenaica in North Africa.
regions.detail: Paul’s ship shelters along Crete in Acts 27. Paul leaves Titus in Crete to appoint elders (Titus 1:5).
regions.uncertainty: The shape is a simple outline of the island. Cyrenaica is not marked.

regions.name: Italy
regions.summary: Italy was the home region of Rome. It had a special status among Roman lands.
regions.detail: Paul lands at Puteoli and goes on to Rome (Acts 28). Hebrews 13:24 sends greetings from the Italians.
regions.uncertainty: The shape is a simple outline of the peninsula.

guides.title: Galatians: context and evidence
guides.description: Explore the book’s larger concerns through selected passages and relevant evidence.

steps.title: Shared recognition fails when fear divides the meal
steps.text: Verse 12 gives the facts: Peter ate with Gentiles and then withdrew in fear. Verse 13 says the other Jewish believers and Barnabas followed him. Verse 14 names the fault: not walking by the truth of the good news. Paul answers “before them all.” His question points to the gap. Peter himself had lived like a Gentile. Now his withdrawal pressed Gentiles to live like Jews.

steps.title: Promise and shared inheritance answer the demand for another membership sign
steps.text: The dispute is who counts as Abraham’s offspring and heir. Verse 16 says the promised offspring is Christ. Verse 17 says the later law cannot cancel that promise. Verses 26–28 say all who are baptized into Christ are one in him. Verse 29 draws the conclusion in two steps. If they belong to Christ, they are Abraham’s offspring. If offspring, they are heirs by promise.

steps.title: Paul turns a family account into an argument about the disputed promise
steps.text: Verse 21 addresses those who want to be under the law. Paul answers them from the law’s own account of Abraham (verse 22). Verse 24 says plainly that he reads it as an allegory. The two women stand for two covenants, and Hagar stands for Sinai. Verse 26 sets the free Jerusalem above against her. This is Paul’s comparison for this dispute, not a verdict on a people. Verse 31 gives its point: believers are children of the free woman.

steps.title: Freedom becomes service through love rather than permission to consume others
steps.text: Verse 1 said Christ set them free and warned against a yoke of bondage. Verse 13 guards that freedom from the other side. Freedom must not become an opening for the flesh. The verse then tells free people to be servants to one another. Love is the means. Verse 14 gives the reason: the whole law is fulfilled in loving a neighbor. Verse 15 shows the alternative: biting and devouring until they consume each other.

chapterMaps.note: Lines join the places Galatians names, in order. They do not trace real roads or sea lanes.
chapterMaps.narrative: Paul writes to the assemblies of Galatia as an apostle sent by Jesus Christ. He gives no thanks. He is amazed that they are turning so quickly to a different good news. He says anyone who brings another message is cursed. His message did not come from a human source. He once persecuted the assembly and advanced in Judaism. God called him, and he went to Arabia, not to Jerusalem. After three years he visited Peter for fifteen days and saw James.
chapterMaps.limits: Lines join the places Galatians names, in order. They do not trace real roads or sea lanes.

chapterMaps.note: Lines join the places Galatians names, in order. They do not trace real roads or sea lanes.
chapterMaps.narrative: After fourteen years Paul goes to Jerusalem with Barnabas and Titus. Titus, a Greek, is not forced to be circumcised. James, Peter, and John give Paul and Barnabas the right hand of fellowship. They ask only that he remember the poor. In Antioch Peter eats with Gentiles, then draws back when men come from James. Barnabas is carried along too. Paul rebukes Peter before everyone. He says a person is justified by faith in Christ, not by law.
chapterMaps.limits: Lines join the places Galatians names, in order. They do not trace real roads or sea lanes.

chapterMaps.note: Markers show the cities Paul names in his memories. Mount Sinai and the Jerusalem above have no point.
chapterMaps.narrative: Paul calls the Galatians foolish and asks how they received the Spirit. It was by hearing with faith, not by works of the law. Abraham believed God, and those of faith are his children. The law curses all who fail to keep it, and Christ redeemed us. The promise to Abraham came 430 years before the law. The law cannot cancel it. The law was a tutor to bring us to Christ. In Christ there is neither Jew nor Greek, slave nor free, male nor female.
chapterMaps.limits: Markers show the cities Paul names in his memories. Mount Sinai and the Jerusalem above have no point.

chapterMaps.note: Markers show the cities Paul names in his memories. Mount Sinai and the Jerusalem above have no point.
chapterMaps.narrative: Paul says an heir who is a child is no different from a servant. God sent his Son, born of a woman, to redeem those under the law. Now they are sons and call God Abba, Father. He asks why they turn back to weak principles and observe days and seasons. He recalls how they welcomed him when he was ill. He is in labor again until Christ is formed in them. Then he tells of Abraham’s two sons, by Hagar and by the free woman. He says believers are children of the free woman.
chapterMaps.limits: Markers show the cities Paul names in his memories. Mount Sinai and the Jerusalem above have no point.

chapterMaps.note: Markers show the cities Paul names in his memories. Mount Sinai and the Jerusalem above have no point.
chapterMaps.narrative: Paul tells the Galatians to stand firm in freedom. If they accept circumcision, they must keep the whole law. What counts is faith working through love. He says a little yeast leavens the whole lump. They were called to freedom, to serve one another through love. The whole law is fulfilled in loving a neighbor as oneself. He lists the works of the flesh and then the fruit of the Spirit. The fruit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith, gentleness, and self-control.
chapterMaps.limits: Markers show the cities Paul names in his memories. Mount Sinai and the Jerusalem above have no point.

chapterMaps.note: Markers show the cities Paul names in his memories. Mount Sinai and the Jerusalem above have no point.
chapterMaps.narrative: Paul tells the spiritual to restore gently anyone caught in a fault. They should bear one another’s burdens. Each should test his own work and carry his own load. A person reaps what he sows, to the flesh or to the Spirit. They should not grow tired of doing good, especially to the household of faith. Paul writes the ending in large letters with his own hand. He says those pressing circumcision want to avoid persecution. He will boast only in the cross, and a new creation is what counts.
